messages.subject: SpectronauttoMSstatsFormat()
messages.body_plain:
Hi MSstats maintainers,

I discovered the following function in the MSstats 3.6 vignette:

SpectronauttoMSstatsFormat {MSstats}R Documentation
Generate MSstats required input format for Spectronaut output
Description

Convert Spectronaut output into the required input format for MSstats.
Usage
SpectronauttoMSstatsFormat(input,
      summaryforMultipleRows=max)
Arguments
input

name of Spectronaut output, which is long-format. ProteinName, PeptideSequence, PrecursorCharge, FragmentIon, ProductCharge, IsotopeLabelType, Condition, BioReplicate, Run, Intensity, F.ExcludedFromQuantification are required. Rows with F.ExcludedFromQuantification=True will be removed.
summaryforMultipleRows

max(default) or sum - when there are multiple measurements for certain feature and certain run, use highest or sum of multiple intensities.
Author(s)

Meena Choi, Olga Vitek.

and I was wondering what it does and which input (Spectronaut Report) it actually expects. There is indeed a Spectronaut export scheme for MSstats, but the contained data is already collapsed on the peptide level (no fragment level AUC), so not really what one would like to use according to Olga. Is anyone of you in contact with Biognosys? Since Spectronaut 10 there is also a MSstats fragment ion report, but the export scheme did not work when I tested it recently. Would be great if you could start talking to each other, regarding I/O formats. I used MSstats together with Spectronaut output twice and each time it took a considerable amount of time to transit the data. Would be great if this could be made easier in the future.

Greetings,
Tobi

But I really would like to make sure we are on the same page: Different precursors of the same peptide - in the absence of noise or factors like unexpected modifications - should behave alike in a linear regression? Thought experiment: I would buy 10 synthetic peptides, mix them, pipette a linear dilution series and measure all available precursors by DIA. Will the slope be the same for peptide i in z = 2, 3 , 4, ... or can peptide i | z=2 be different from peptide i | z=3 given the signals allow a high quality regression for both charges. Does the response factor depend on z?

Greetings,

messages.subject: Re: nature of the response factor or how to model it correctly
messages.subject_clean: nature of the response factor or how to model it correctly
messages.body_plain:
Dear Tobias,

I am not sure which linear regression you have in mind. See, e.g. the figure on p.15 of the user manual http://msstats.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/MSstats_v3.6_manual.pdf

All the features that represent a protein (in your case, a peptide) are expected to have same *systematic* patterns of variation between the runs. I.e., they are expected to systematically go up and down between the runs in the same manner, as in the left part of the figure.  All the deviations from this systematic up and down variation is assumed to be non-systematic, irreproducible, noise. The summarization step finds a consensus pattern of the systematic variation, while accounting for censored values, missing values, and outliers, as shown in the right part of the figure.

HTH
Olga

messages.body_plain:
It's possible to do that - for example, if you want to compare between average of C2 and C3 and average of C1, (C3+C2)/2-C1 as formula, set ‘-1’ for C1, ‘0.5’ for C2 and ‘0.5’ for C3, and ‘0’ for rest of groups. See more details on page 19 of the manual
http://msstats.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/MSstats_v3.6_manual.pdf

HTH
Tsung-Heng

messages.body_plain:
Hi Meena,

I looked into the manual regarding SpectronauttoMSstatsFormat(). There it says:

"First, it uses only noloss from F.FrgLossType. If not, multiple measurements for each feature and run can be happend."

I don't think this is a smart way to go, because it means that in the likely case that the strongest fragment ion is generated by water-loos or ammonium-loss, MSstats will simply ignore it! One might might indeed like to make sure that not several fragment ions originating from the same y- or b-ion are selected for quantification (e.g. y7-noloss and y7-H20-loss), but that would require a different filter function.

A second observation:

Spectronaut considers replicate IDs only unique within sample groups (grouped according to conditions). I thought that MSstats requires a unique BioReplicate ID across all samples, otherwise it would interpret these replicates as technical replicates. The function reports all peptides to be unique in proteins...well, looking at the PG.ProteinAccessions column I would argue: Yes, technically they are, because Spectronaut reports a ;-separated  list of protein ACCs in this field. So the peptides are only unique after protein grouping. Is that really what you want? This would accordingly give you protein group inference in the end, not a protein inference.

Greetings,
Tobi

messages.body_plain:
To add to Tsung-Heng's comments: even though in your example MSstats and limma use the same input, these are different models (in particular with respect to variance estimation) and therefore produce different results. If you would like to know all the details, please join us at the May Institute https://computationalproteomics.ccis.northeastern.edu/ where we will discuss this extensively.

HTH
Olga
